title: Why Beaches Never Settle
question: Why does a beach keep changing shape instead of staying put?
hook: The waves on a beach change in an instant, but the sand is always running to catch up.
idea: A beach reshapes only by moving sediment, which takes time, and since the forces on it keep changing it never reaches a final shape.

beats.prompt: A steep beach of coarse sand is hit by a strong storm with steep waves. What happens to its shape?

choices.label: It flattens as sand moves offshore
It gets steeper as waves throw sand up
choices.feedback: Calm waves on coarse sand can leave material high on the beach, but storm waves move sediment the other way, offshore.

choices.label: Nothing changes; coarse sand is too heavy
choices.feedback: Coarse grains are heavier, yet storms still shift them; beach states change with wave energy.

beats.explain: Changes in wave energy drive changes in beach state: storms flatten reflective beaches by carrying sediment offshore, making them more dissipative.

beats.prompt: Sort each feature into the beach type it belongs to.
beats.explain: Sediment size and slope go together: fine sand makes flat beaches with spilling waves, coarse sand makes steep beaches with surging waves.

beats.prompt: Match each beach setting to the water motion that dominates near the bottom there.
pairs: Incident waves and subharmonic edge waves
Inner surf zone of a highly dissipative beach
beats.explain: Which currents rule near the seabed depends on the beach state.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Moving water responds the instant a beach changes shape.
The beach itself can only change by moving sediment.
Moving sediment takes no time, so the beach keeps pace with the waves exactly.
Since the forcing keeps changing, the beach never reaches equilibrium.
beats.explain: Sediment takes a finite time to move, so the beach's response always lags behind the waves rather than keeping pace.
